tldr: To eliminate the overly cautious slowness typical of teleoperation, this new framework estimates phase-wise manipulation tempo from egocentric human videos of the same task and retimes robot action sequences for imitation learning. In real-world experiments, it improved task success rate by an average of 25 percentage points while reducing execution time by 36.5%.
hero_caption: Overall processing pipeline of EgoSpeedUp. Slow robot demonstrations and fast human task videos are segmented and aligned into the same manipulation phases (P0 to P3), and target tempos for the robot are computed from the duration ratios of each phase. By performing behavior cloning (BC) using action targets resampled according to these tempos, the robot learns fast policies that preserve natural human pacing.
overview:
Imitation learning is a standard approach for enabling robots to acquire complex manipulation skills, but it has a major weakness: it faithfully copies the excessive slowness and awkwardness of teleoperated demonstration data. When humans perform tasks directly with their own hands, they move quickly and fluidly. In contrast, teleoperators tend to move cautiously and slowly to avoid failures.

Existing acceleration methods attempt to estimate how much to accelerate using robot-side information—such as policy predictive uncertainty or motion complexity—or adjust speeds within a predefined range of acceleration factors. However, automatically determining task-appropriate manipulation tempo—specifically, how fast each manipulation phase should progress—without an external reference has been extremely difficult.

To address this, the authors focused on the fact that natural human manual manipulation inherently embeds the optimal phase-wise tempo and pacing. The proposed framework, EgoSpeedUp, aligns egocentric human manipulation videos with robot demonstrations across corresponding task phases and estimates target phase-wise tempos from the ratio of human-to-robot step counts. It then resamples future action targets along the temporal dimension according to this tempo while leaving the robot's observations unchanged during training.

When evaluated on a real UR5e robot across two tasks with vastly different dynamical properties—straightening a rope and carrying a block tower—EgoSpeedUp automatically acquired appropriate pacing without manual hyperparameter tuning of acceleration rates. As a result, it improved task success rate by an average of 25 percentage points compared to conventional methods while reducing successful execution time by 36.5%.
contributions: Proposed a framework that leverages duration ratios from natural human hand-manipulation videos as phase-wise temporal supervision for robot imitation learning.

Established a mechanism to monotonically align human videos and robot trajectories based on physical interaction events, determining episode- and phase-wise target tempos without manual acceleration range tuning.

Demonstrated on real-robot hardware across both dynamic-friendly and delicacy-requiring tasks that the method simultaneously achieves higher success rates and substantial reductions in execution time.

sections.heading: Why are robots overly cautious? Learning pacing from human manipulation
sections.summary: Teleoperated demonstrations tend to be cautious, and imitation-learned policies inherit this slow tempo. EgoSpeedUp transfers phase-wise execution durations from human manual manipulation to robots as temporal supervision, learning policies that run at appropriate speeds without manual tuning.
sections.details:
With the rise of imitation learning, robots can now perform a diverse range of manipulation skills. However, when executing trained policies, their movements are often frustratingly slow compared to a human performing the task directly. The root cause lies in data collection: during teleoperation, human operators move overly cautiously and slowly due to interface constraints and fear of failure.

Prior studies have certainly attempted faster-than-demonstration execution. Yet, they rely on robot-side uncertainty or predefined tempo multipliers (e.g., 2x to 4x), lacking an objective reference for how fast a specific moment of a task should naturally progress. Appropriate speeds differ drastically across tasks and manipulation phases.

Here, the authors turned their attention to human movement itself. Humans intuitively modulate their movement timing depending on precision requirements and physical dynamics. For instance, when straightening a bent rope, humans quickly whip their wrist to extend the rope efficiently. The core idea of this work is that by using how fast a human would perform each phase as a temporal reference (temporal supervision), robots can naturally acquire both safe and fast manipulation tempos.

captions.F1: Conceptual diagram of EgoSpeedUp. Conventional teleoperation demonstrations (top) are slow and cautious throughout. In contrast, direct human execution (middle) naturally modulates pacing across phases, such as whipping the rope (Phase 2) roughly 3x faster. EgoSpeedUp (bottom) detects these tempo differences and transfers them into the robot's manipulation phases.

sections.heading: At the intersection of robot acceleration and human video utilization
sections.summary: Existing faster-than-demonstration methods rely on robot-side signals or pre-set acceleration ranges. Meanwhile, human videos have been used for visual representations and cross-embodiment transfer, but have not been explicitly utilized as references for task tempo.
sections.details:
### II-A Faster-than-Demonstration Robot Policies
Simply speeding up demonstration replay causes failures during contact phases where high precision is required. Earlier studies have addressed this by estimating high-precision segments from policy uncertainty (entropy) to accelerate only low-precision segments, modulating speed based on kinematic complexity, or determining acceleration segments through semantic reasoning. Other approaches pretrain on speed-augmented demonstrations before using reinforcement learning to encourage speedup, or select targets across multiple time horizons based on prediction errors. However, all these methods depend on robot-side information or hard-coded search bounds, lacking an external reference for what constitutes a task-appropriate execution tempo.

### II-B Human Videos in Robot Learning
Videos of humans performing tasks have served as rich sources of visual and semantic information for pretraining visual representations, inferring task intent, and extracting object motion trajectories. In recent years, research has actively explored direct manipulation transfer from egocentric videos to robots and cross-embodiment learning mapping hand trajectories to robot arms. However, these focus on transferring 'what to do' (actions and representations), leaving open the idea of using human video as a temporal guide for 'how fast each phase should progress.'

sections.heading: Preliminaries: Action chunking and tempo-based retiming
sections.summary: The proposed method builds on action-chunking imitation learning, which predicts future action sequences from current observations in one shot. It formulates a retiming mechanism that resamples actions along time to accelerate execution without altering the policy's predictive structure.
sections.details:
### III-A Imitation Learning with Action Chunking
Modern imitation learning often adopts action chunking, where instead of predicting actions step by step, the policy predicts a sequence of future $H$-step actions $\mathbf{A}_t = [a_t, a_{t+1}, \dots, a_{t+H-1}]$ all at once given current observation $o_t$. Standard behavior cloning (BC) learns action sequences at the original time intervals of the collected robot demonstrations; if the demonstrations are slow, the learned policy is equally slow.

### III-B Tempo-Based Action Retiming
One way to increase execution speed without altering chunk horizon $H$ is to look ahead in time and resample future action targets. Given tempo factor $v \ge 1$, each element of the retimed action sequence is queried from demonstration timestamp $t + v \cdot k$ for $k \in \{0, \dots, H-1\}$ (using linear interpolation for non-integer indices). When $v=1$, it retains the nominal speed; when $v>1$, farther future actions are selected, training the robot to advance the task faster within the same duration. The key challenge is how to determine $v$, which EgoSpeedUp derives directly from human manual demonstrations.

sections.heading: EgoSpeedUp: Aligning human and robot phases to extract tempo
sections.summary: Human and robot demonstrations are segmented into shared phases, and step count ratios for each phase are calculated via monotonic phase matching. Target tempo factors are determined from the mean ratio across multiple demonstrations, and behavior cloning is trained on retimed robot action targets.
sections.details:
### IV-A Temporal Alignment between Humans and Robots
Comparing only the total duration of the entire task provides just a single uniform speedup factor, losing the distinction between delicate phases and phases that should be rushed. Therefore, the task is divided into an ordered sequence of $P$ shared phases such as Approach, Grasp, Manipulation, and Release. Coarse semantic boundaries are first extracted using a VLM-based annotation approach called Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT), and then refined based on physical interaction events.
- Robot side: Boundaries are defined by gripper open/close signals and the onset of object manipulation events (e.g., the moment the rope starts moving).
- Human side: Hand keypoints from WiLoR and RGB-D depth track 3D thumb-index fingertip distance to detect grasp opening/closing, while SAM 2 tracks the object to detect contact, grasp, and onset of coupled object motion.
This establishes monotonic phase matching that preserves the temporal sequence order between human and robot demonstrations.

### IV-B Human-Informed Target Tempo Factor Estimation
For each aligned phase $p$, the step length ratio $r_{e,p,m} = \ell^R_{e,p} / \ell^H_{m,p}$ is computed between robot episode $e$ step length $\ell^R_{e,p}$ and human demonstration $m$ step length $\ell^H_{m,p}$. A ratio greater than 1 indicates that the human completed that phase faster. The deterministic target tempo $\hat{v}_{e,p}$ for that robot episode and phase is obtained by averaging these ratios across all $M$ human demonstrations and clipping the lower bound at 1.0.

### IV-C Tempo-Guided Action Target Generation and Training
During training, future action chunks are retimed using the tempo $v_{e,t}$ corresponding to the phase at timestamp $t$. Robot input observations $o_{e,t}$ remain at their original timestamps, while only the predicted target action labels are shifted forward according to the tempo. The policy backbone employs ManiFlow based on Flow Matching. At inference time, no phase estimator or tempo reference is needed; the policy runs as a standard visuomotor policy, generating action chunks directly from visual and proprioceptive inputs.

sections.heading: Real-robot evaluation: Testing dynamic rope and delicate blocks
sections.summary: EgoSpeedUp was tested on a UR5e robot on rope straightening and two-tier block transport tasks. It significantly outperformed fixed-speedup and existing acceleration baselines, achieving a 2.63x speedup on Rope and an 85% success rate on Block.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
- Hardware: UR5e manipulator, Robotiq Hand-E gripper, and two Intel RealSense D435 cameras (one third-person scene view, one wrist-mounted). Observations consist of RGB images from both cameras (224x224, 2 frames) and proprioception; the output is a 7D action (6 joint position targets + gripper command).
- Task Design: Two tasks with contrasting temporal demands were evaluated.
  1. Rope (Rope Straightening): Grasp a curved rope and pull it straight. Fast, dynamic pulling motions are beneficial.
  2. Block (Block Placement): Transport a yellow base block stacked with two red blocks into a target tray without toppling the tower. Excessive acceleration causes tower collapse, requiring caution.
- Data Collection: For each task, 80 teleoperated robot demonstrations were collected using a 3D mouse (at 10Hz), alongside 40 egocentric human manipulation videos (at 20Hz).
- Baselines: Compared against Nominal (trained on raw demos), fixed acceleration (Global 2x / 4x), DemoSpeedup (switching between 2x and 4x based on uncertainty), SpeedAug-prior (trained on 1x to 3x speed-augmented data), and AutoSpeed (selecting tempo between 0.8x and 2.2x based on prediction error).

### V-B Quantitative Results
Across both tasks (20 trials per method across 2 tasks), EgoSpeedUp achieved the highest overall success rate of 82.5% and a 1.58x total speedup over Nominal. While Global 4x and DemoSpeedup were over 2.6x faster, their success rates plummeted to 40.0%. AutoSpeed achieved only a 67.5% success rate without accelerating execution (0.97x speedup).
- Rope Task: EgoSpeedUp raised the success rate from 60% to 80% while dramatically reducing average successful execution time from 14.76s to 5.60s (a 2.63x speedup).
- Block Task: In this task where over-acceleration is fatal, EgoSpeedUp modestly reduced time from 14.48s to 12.89s (1.12x speedup) while boosting the success rate from 55% to 85%.

### V-C Ablations and Analysis
- Phase-wise vs. Global: Applying a single uniform tempo ratio across the entire task lowered success rate by 17.5 pp.
- Number of Human Demos: Reducing reference videos from 40 down to 5 or 10 decreased success rate by 17.5 to 22.5 pp, confirming that diverse human references are needed to cover initial configuration variations.
- Aggregation Method: Replacing the mean ratio with the median dropped success rate by 20.0 pp.
- Failure Analysis: On Rope, grasping failures were the primary error mode; EgoSpeedUp significantly reduced them. On Block, baseline methods frequently dropped or collapsed the stacked blocks during transport, whereas EgoSpeedUp maintained stable transportation.

captions.F3: Phase segmentation and computed average tempo ratios for Rope and Block tasks. For Rope, large speedups were assigned to approach (P0, 7.38x) and straightening (P2, 3.59x). In contrast, for the delicate Block task, gentle tempos between 1.0x and 1.3x were automatically assigned across all phases.
captions.F5: Primary failure modes and number of failed trials per phase. Out of 20 trials, aggressive acceleration baselines (Global 4x, DemoSpeedup, SpeedAug) failed frequently due to grasping errors or toppling blocks. EgoSpeedUp kept failures exceptionally low: only 4 on Rope and 3 on Block.

sections.heading: Discussion and future outlook: Limitations of fixed phases and beyond
sections.summary: While the framework shows powerful results with a simple setup, its assumptions of a single sequential phase progression and inability to adjust speeds dynamically within phases represent key limitations.
sections.details:
The strength of EgoSpeedUp lies in extracting task-appropriate velocity profiles from natural human hand manipulation videos without complex hyperparameter search. However, several limitations remain.

First, the method assumes that human and robot demonstrations follow the same ordered sequence of phases. For unstructured tasks involving retries, branching, or cyclical behaviors, phase-level matching must be replaced or extended with trajectory-level alignment techniques.

Second, assigning a single deterministic tempo factor to each phase prevents fine-grained acceleration/deceleration within a phase or online adaptation to runtime state changes. Moving forward, combining human tempo priors with policy uncertainty or state-adaptive velocity selection mechanisms could enable more flexible and responsive speed control.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Human manipulation is the best textbook for speed
sections.summary: EgoSpeedUp extracts phase-wise manipulation tempos from egocentric human videos to retime robot action targets for imitation learning. Real-world tasks proved that human manipulation tempo serves as an effective benchmark for balancing safety and speed.
sections.details:
This paper presented EgoSpeedUp, a framework designed to resolve the overly slow execution of policies trained via imitation learning. By aligning human and robot demonstrations phase by phase and applying target tempos derived from duration ratios to action chunk retiming, robots learn policies with human-informed pacing at zero additional inference cost.

Real-robot experiments demonstrated that EgoSpeedUp adapts execution speed according to task demands—substantially accelerating the rope task where dynamic motions help, while maintaining high reliability in the block task where delicate transport is essential. These results clearly show that the subtle timing information in everyday human manual actions provides a powerful external reference for making robot policies both faster and more reliable.

takeaways: While teleoperated robot demonstrations tend to be overly conservative, using phase duration ratios from natural human hand-manipulation videos allows robots to naturally learn task-appropriate pacing.

Estimating tempo and retiming actions phase by phase (e.g., approach vs. contact) rather than applying a single uniform multiplier across the whole task is decisive for maintaining high success rates.

At inference time, phase detection and tempo calculation are completely unnecessary; the robot runs at high speed using a standard visuomotor policy (such as ManiFlow), making it easy to deploy on real systems.
limitations: Assumes tasks follow a predefined, strictly ordered phase sequence (e.g., Approach -> Grasp -> Manipulate -> Release); extending it to unstructured tasks with branching or retries requires future work.
Applies a constant tempo factor within each phase, meaning it lacks state-dependent dynamic speed adaptation to slow down in real time when facing unexpected disturbances or misalignments.
Relies on human hand and object tracking (WiLoR and SAM 2) combined with depth cameras to detect contact events, which may face accuracy challenges in heavily occluded scenes or with tiny objects.
